mini_cube_ps2.8.1.bgcode
mini_cube_b.bgcode

Binary G-code test files taken from Prusa Research's libbgcode, at
https://github.com/prusa3d/libbgcode (tests/data), which is licensed under the
GNU Affero General Public License v3.0.

They are kept here so the decoder can be checked against files produced by the
reference implementation rather than by this project. The matching ASCII files
from that repository are not included; the expected decoder output is pinned as
a length and CRC32 in tests/binary_gcode.rs instead.


objects_2walls_bambu.gcode.zst
objects_manywalls_bambu.gcode.zst

One plate of the primitives Bambu Studio adds from its right-click menu — cube,
sphere, cone, cylinder and the rest — sliced with Bambu Studio 02.08.02.61 for
a 0.4 mm nozzle at 0.2 mm layers, 0.45 mm inner and 0.42 mm outer walls,
wall_sequence "inner wall/outer wall", which is the stock order and lays the
visible wall down last. One asks for 2 walls and the other for a thousand, so
the same shapes are carried by one hidden wall in the first and by as many as
their geometry allows in the second. Nothing here is anyone's design: they are
the solids the slicer generates on demand.

Both are an eight-layer window — layers 144 to 151, kept behind the file's own
header and config block — and compressed with zstd. A nozzle replay needs a
real slicer's travels, arcs, wipes, seam gaps and gap fill, and none of that
survives being written by hand.

The window is where it is because the domes are there. A Benchy stood here
before and was the wrong subject: its hull is near vertical, so the surface
transform had almost nothing to work on, and a bound on how deep a crest it
leaves passed at a quarter of a layer on that fixture and was false by a factor
of three on the whole file. A fixture that does not reach the feature under
test is worse than none. This window carries 27 top-surface regions across
eight layers and eight objects.

They are inputs, not expectations. tests/collision.rs runs the binary over them
and replays a nozzle across the result.


baseline.gcode.zst, and the twenty-four named after the one setting each
changes: arachne, arachne-thinwall, fuzzy-skin, gapfill-off,
infill-solid, infill-solid-1wall, infill-solid-2walls, infill-solid-zigzag,
inner-outer-inner, layer-max, layer-thin, nasty-combo, no-arcs, no-prime-tower,
no-zhop, outer-first, scarf-seam, seam-back, seam-random, walls-1, walls-3,
walls-6, zhop-normal, zhop-spiral.

One plate, sliced twenty-eight ways — and **the only fixture set here that can
be made again.** It is `tests/fixtures/generator/manyparts.3mf`: fourteen parts
of real modelling, sliced by Bambu Studio 02.08.02.61 for a **Bambu Lab P1S
with a 0.4 mm nozzle at 0.2 mm layers**. The script that does it sits beside
the plate, and a plain run of it rewrites exactly these twenty-eight files:

```sh
tests/fixtures/generator/generate.py "flatpak run com.bambulab.BambuStudio"
```

`baseline.gcode.zst` is the profile as saved: 2 walls, classic generator,
`wall_sequence` "inner wall/outer wall", arc fitting on, `z_hop` 0.4 mm Auto
Lift, aligned seam, printed by layer. **Every other file changes exactly one
setting**, and the setting is in the name — except `nasty-combo.gcode.zst`,
which turns on everything awkward at once.

Each is checked against the baseline on the way out, twice, which is the rule
`generate.py` exists to enforce: a fixture that does not reach the feature it
is named for is worse than no fixture, because it reports a pass nobody earned.
The G-code must come back naming the new value in its own settings block —
Bambu Studio drops a number where that file stores strings, and takes a value
it does not recognise without a word — and what the binary does with it must
move off the baseline's own counts by more than the slicer's run-to-run noise.

They are windows, not whole plates: layers 60 to 75, with the file's own head
kept in front so the start G-code, the settings block and the machine's own
below-the-bed nozzle wipe are all still there. Whole plates come to 14.9 MB.
Layers 60 to 75 keep every object that reaches that high and reach both
transforms: **788 loops, 325 of them raised, and 452 surface moves** on the
baseline. The `infill-solid*` four are eight layers rather than sixteen, since
a plate whose fill is laid solid is half as much G-code again per layer.

The plate earned its keep on the first run. Two faults in this binary, both
of them present on `main`, neither of them reachable from any other fixture
here:

- `--bricks` reordered a wall and left a **different `; LINE_WIDTH:` standing
  over the regions behind it**. The width is modal — a slicer states it once
  and the regions behind it inherit it — so the sparse infill, which states
  none of its own, came out under the outer wall's. Measured: **52066 mm of
  165303 mm, a third of the file's beads, drawn at a width the slicer did not
  declare for it.**
- Bambu writes `G1 X.. Y.. E0` part-way round a loop of a wall: the same point
  as the bead before it, and no filament. Read as a travel it **cut the ring in
  two**, so the halves were contoured, numbered and raised apart — half a layer
  of step in the middle of one wall — and the half that was reordered carried
  the slicer's stationary move with it.

`no-prime-tower.gcode.zst` is the one variant that reaches nothing: this plate
prints one filament and Bambu builds no tower for it, so the file differs from
the baseline in its settings block and nowhere else. It is kept because the
setting is worth pinning where it is stated, and the script marks it out as
`settings only` when it writes the set.

`infill-solid.gcode.zst`, `-1wall`, `-2walls`, `-zigzag`

The same plate with its fill laid **solid** instead of at 15%: `sparse_infill_density` 100%, and `wall_loops` 0, 1 and 2. Fourteen objects, eight layers each,
none of them a wall stack for most of its body. They are here because a fill at
full density is a wall in everything but its label — its strands are laid
against each other, and with `wall_loops = 0` the outermost of them is the
part's visible face. `--bricks` used to do nothing at all on one of these.

`infill-solid-zigzag` is the negative control, and is stored so that the
transform is held to declining it rather than reaching it. `concentric` and
`zig-zag` are the only two patterns Bambu Studio will lay at full density at
all — asked for `grid`, `line` or `rectilinear` it exits 238 with
`doesn't work at 100% density` — and of the two only the concentric one is a
stack of rings: measured on this plate, a layer of it is 455 runs every one of
which closes within 0.06 mm, against 46 open runs whose ends are 7 to 35 mm
apart. `zig-zag` is also **rotated a quarter turn every layer** — layer 62 runs
at 45° and layer 63 at 135°, where the concentric fill runs at 90° and 0° — so
a raised strand has nothing at the same place above it and the next layer cuts
straight through the ridge. `generate.py` marks that variant `expects="declined"`
and fails the run if any loop is raised on it.

The three concentric ones are the positive cases at the three wall counts. What
they prove is the plate's own counts — 2 walls of a fourteen-object plate
cannot raise 1264 loops on their own — and the `plates.rs` test over each pins
that the run is still sound G-code and still carries every region marker. Over
their eight layers `infill-solid` reports 3460 loops with 1224 raised,
`-1wall` 3534 with 1211, `-2walls` 3523 with 1264, against the same plate at
15% fill reporting 1095 and 475.

Regenerating them, and the traps in doing so, is
`.github/skills/fixtures-generation/SKILL.md`.

Two variants are deliberately absent. `print_sequence = by object` and
`spiral_mode` both need a plate this one is not — sequential printing refuses
these objects as too tall and too close, and spiral vase refuses more than one
object. `ironing_type` will not take on this project at any of its four values.
A tool change is absent too, and cannot be patched in: this plate's process
profile is written for a P1S, and pointing the machine at a two-nozzle H2D gets
`process not compatible with printer`, exit -17. Absolute `E` is absent for a
quieter reason — `use_relative_e_distances = 0` is accepted and echoed back
while the G-code comes out with `M83` and relative filament anyway.

The plate is Bambu Studio's own built-in shapes, and it carries a 3DBenchy by
Creative Tools, CC BY-ND 4.0 (unmodified).



support.gcode.zst, support-grid.gcode.zst

Two windows of the plate above with supports switched on: the one region
nothing else here carries, and the one thing in this tool that may touch
nothing — material printed to be broken off, one bead wide, tall and unbraced,
with no wall to raise and nothing above a step to meet.

They are the two shapes a wall can meet support in. `support` is the plate's
own `support_type` of `tree(auto)`, which stands *beside* a wall — 99 support
regions inside its window, 365 loops and 122 of them raised, in eight layers.
`support-grid.gcode.zst` is `normal(auto)` in `grid`, which stands *under* the
walls: 31 support regions and 21 of `Support interface`, and **0 loops raised
out of 211**, because a wall laid on support is held flat. Both are needed; the
rule that holds that wall flat is not visible from the tree shape alone.

These are the two fixtures behind the defect history here — 5136 wall beads
once came out under the support's own `; FEATURE:` marker and so at its fan
speed, and 8902 retractions were added to a file with 13234. Both were found on
a real tree-support print that stood here in their place. These two are sliced
from the plate beside the generator instead, so they can be made again; the
trouble is that Bambu will not slice supports on that plate as saved — the
objects sit close enough that their tree supports run into each other, exit -101
— so `generate.py` arranges it first (`--arrange 1`) and stores the first of
the two plates that arrangement produces.


cone.gcode.zst

A 24-layer window of a real funnel — a thin cone whose wall walks outward by a
fraction of a bead every layer, kept behind the file's own header and config
block.

Nothing else here has that shape, and it is the shape that matters: on a wall
that stacks, a loop either sits over the raise below it or it does not, and a
threshold on the share of its path that does answers correctly. On a wall that
walks, every loop sits partly over the raise, and a threshold rounds all of
them the same way. Measured on this window, v3.0.1 said it added 1.37% of
filament and the part lost 8.01%.


coupon.gcode.zst

An eight-layer window of a real test coupon — a flat link with two holes
through it — kept behind the file's own header and config block.

It is here because a top surface with holes in it is the shape where the
coverage answer flips back and forth along one path: the layer above closes
over the surface at every hole, and a bead running past one grazes the cells
that close it. `--bricks --zaa` wrote 25 beads standing above both their
neighbours more steeply than one in one, against none for either transform on
its own — bricking moves the visible wall inward, so its path meets those
cells at a different angle. They are the dots a preview draws around the holes.
